title: Burst concurrency slotting trace notes
content:
Summary:
This is a working log of the April trace sweep focused on burst concurrency slotting — how incoming requests are assigned 'concurrency slots' (logical serving capacity) and how that interacts with CUDA stream priority, async copies, and microbatch handoff. We observed sporadic 95th/99th tail spikes that correlate with slot exhaustion events; this doc collects captures, hypotheses, and quick experiments to reproduce and mitigate.

Background / why we care:
- Our runtime allows a limited number of in-flight 'concurrency slots' per model instance to control memory and KV-cache pressure.
- During short bursts (traffic spikes < 1s), the scheduler seems to serialize some decoder kernels even though GPUs were not fully occupied overall.
- Result: noisy tail latencies for bursty requests (chat-type workloads).

Hypothesis (short):
1) Slot allocation currently batches slot handoff at the CPU scheduler level in coarse quanta (~4-8ms), causing multiple microbatches to queue and then enter the GPU simultaneously, producing microbursting inside the GPU driver (kernel launch serialization + stream preemption).
2) When async H2D copies are in-flight, the runtime demotes stream priorities; the combination of demotions + coarse slot handoff makes some decoder_kernels wait on a preemption window, creating 10-30ms bumps.
3) KV-cache prefetch operations (prefix_cache_lookup and kv_fetch kernels) occasionally steal slots because they pin memory and increment the in-flight counter while performing host synchronization in our current prefetch mode.

Experiment captures (Nsight CLI + lightweight traces):
- trace id: nsight-3e7a1bdc (captured 2025-04-10 14:02:10 UTC)
- capture notes: 30s window, model L=2048, microbatch size=1, concurrency_limit=12, burst traffic injection: Poisson mean 30 rps with 100ms spike bursts.
- nvprof/nvtx markers added around: scheduler.allocate_slot(), scheduler.release_slot(), kv_cache.prefetch_start(), kv_cache.prefetch_end(), async_copy.h2d_start, async_copy.h2d_end, decoder.launch.

Key observations from the timeline (nsight-3e7a1bdc):
- At T+12.4s there is a cluster of 6 decoder.launch kernels back-to-back with ~1ms spacing (kernel-launch-density). GPU SM utilization at that interval is only 45% but there are many short (~0.4ms) kernel invocations. This indicates many tiny kernels serialized rather than fewer fused longer kernels.
- Between T+12.3s and T+12.5s we see scheduler.allocate_slot() NVTX intervals collapse to zero (many slots granted at once) — evidence of coarse-grained CPU-side wake/sched.
- Two async_copy.h2d operations appear with high host CPU CPU_WAIT time; the runtime marked them as high-priority H2D but then lowered the compute-stream priority while the copy was in-progress, causing decoder kernels to launch on a low-prio stream and get preempted by longer kernels.
- Trace shows prefix_cache_lookup kernel holding a pinned memory allocation for ~18ms while waiting on host-side I/O (disk or network). This holds a slot and prevents its release; other requests queue and then enter when slots free, creating a mini-burst.

Quantitative slices (approx):
- 95th tail spike correlation: 85% of spikes coincide with a slot-grant collapse event (many allocations within a 2ms window).
- Average kernel launch latency (when serialized in bursts): 0.38ms; when spread: 0.12ms.
- Extra scheduler-induced queueing adds ~6-20ms to the tail depending on prefetch blocking.

Reproduction steps (mini test harness):
1) start-serving --model small-chat --concurrency-limit 12 --slot-quanta-ms 8 --kv-prefetch-mode pinned_host_sync
2) python tools/loadgen.py --rps 30 --burst 100ms --duration 60s --seed 42
3) capture nsight for 30s starting 10s into the run
Notes: slot-quanta-ms is an instrumentation-only knob added to test different handoff quantum sizes.

Quick experiments run so far:
- Reduce slot-quanta-ms to 1ms: reduces observed serialized launch clusters by ~70%, 95th latency improved from 42ms -> 28ms for this workload. However increases CPU wake frequency and small extra scheduling overhead (worth it for bursty chat paths).
- Change kv-prefetch-mode to async_host (nonblocking DMA + completion callback): reduces slot hold time for prefix_cache_lookup from 18ms -> 2.1ms; combined with slot-quanta 1ms gives best tail reduction.
- Force all async copies to use dedicated copy engine streams (separate from compute streams): reduces preemption-induced stalls but uncovered an L2-bandwidth contention case (marginal).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why do some tiny kernels remain serialized even after we tightened slot-quanta? Hypothesis: CUDA driver coalesces launches when many small launches occur close in time from the same host thread; we might need to introduce micro-batching at the host launch level (group tiny kernels into one fused kernel launch).
- Is pinned memory usage by KV-cache unavoidable for low-copy latency? Could we switch to a pinned-less zero-copy approach for small lookups?
- Are there NUMA effects on the host that make slot handoffs bunched (e.g., wakeups landing on the same core)? Need to run with perf pinned to different CPUs.

Suggested short-term mitigations (can be feature flags):
- slot_quanta_ms = 1 (default for chat workloads)
- kv_prefetch_mode = async_host by default for microbatch=1; add a safety threshold for large batches
- dedicate copy engine streams via config: copy_stream_policy = dedicated
- introduce host-side microbatch fuse: if < X kernels and combined flops < Y then fuse into one launch (experimental)

Longer-term ideas:
- Move to a token-aware slot allocation that considers expected kernel-run-time for the request (pre-annotate requests with expected cost) so slots are not equal-weight.
- Implement a host-level kernel coalescer which batches tiny kernel launches into a single kernel or schedules them spaced to avoid driver coalescing.
- Add per-model NUMA-aware scheduler to avoid wakeup clustering.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: land test flag slot_quanta_ms and run a 48hr A/B against canary (Jira ENG-1287).
- Ben: prototype async_host kv-prefetch change and measure memory pressure and L2 contention.
- Maya: run NUMA affinity experiments and attach perf traces (due 2025-05-07).
- Jonas: review CUDA driver docs for launch coalescing semantics and see if there are recommended host-side spacing strategies.

Notes to future reader / rough TODOs:
- Add representative flamegraphs from nsight traces here (I have exports under /mnt/traces/nsight/3e7a1bdc/ but not checked into Drive).
- Try reproducing on A100 and H100; current captures are on A10x instances.
- Consider adding a synthetic microkernel that simulates many tiny launches to measure driver coalescing threshold.

Appendix: example NVTX timeline excerpt (human readable):
[12.299s] scheduler.allocate_slot start
[12.299s] scheduler.allocate_slot end
[12.300s] scheduler.allocate_slot start
[12.300s] scheduler.allocate_slot end
[12.301s] prefix_cache_lookup start (pinned_alloc)
[12.302s] async_copy.h2d_start
[12.303s] decoder.launch (low-prio)
[12.304s] decoder.launch (low-prio)
[12.305s] decoder.launch (low-prio)
[12.310s] async_copy.h2d_end
[12.317s] prefix_cache_lookup end (release slot)

If helpful we can also capture a smaller 10s nsight trace specifically with CPU perf counters pinned to the scheduler thread.

-- end working notes --
